description: A rather ephemeral and short lived site. In the Late Roman period (mid - late 4th CE), a polygonal structure consisting of six sides with an open entrance facing east onto Watling Street was built around a Late Iron Age grave. While no mound was left, excavators believed that the LIA grave would had a visible mound, as there are others in the vicinity, and the Late Roman shrine builders were seemingly aware of the grave. It is hard to say what the construction of the shrine was like, no architectural features remain other than scattered roof tiles, plaster, and opus sig, leading the excavators to suggest it was a timber framed structure defined by the polygonal ditches, possibly acting as gullies. A double ditch to the north-east ran parallel to Watling Street, and it is suggested this would of extended around to form a temenos around the shrine. A great deal of the finds are loose coins in the polygonal ditches (mainly at the rear), pottery, broken glass, and animal bones in various states of cookedness, from surrounding pits. Largely considered a shrine on morphological grounds, the pottery, coinage, and animal remains allow us to suggest a very narrow date of 340 - 360.
